conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that EMDR therapy can alleviate PTSD symptoms and that the supporting evidence is strong, citing multiple meta-analyses and major clinical guidelines.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion: Yes — EMDR therapy can alleviate PTSD symptoms, and the evidence is strong.**

Multiple systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and clinical guidelines support EMDR as an effective, evidence-based treatment for PTSD:

- A **2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials** (covering 1991–2022) was conducted specifically to verify the efficacy of EMDR in treating PTSD, confirming its clinical effectiveness. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37882423/))

- A **meta-analysis of 26 randomized controlled trials** involving 1,659 participants found EMDR produced a **large effect size (Cohen’s d = 1.08)** for reducing PTSD symptoms. ([Gitnux](https://gitnux.org/emdr-statistics/))

- The **U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs** states that EMDR is “one of the most studied treatments for PTSD” and that “a large number of studies demonstrate it is effective to treat PTSD when administered over approximately 3 months.” ([VA PTSD](https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/txessentials/emdr_pro.asp))

- The **American Psychological Association’s Clinical Practice Guideline** recommends EMDR for the treatment of PTSD. ([APA](https://www.apa.org/ptsd-guideline/treatments/eye-movement-reprocessing))

**Caveat:** Some researchers note that the eye-movement component may not uniquely drive EMDR’s effectiveness; its benefits may stem from therapeutic elements shared with other trauma-focused therapies, leading to its characterization as a “purple hat therapy.” ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_movement_desensitization_and_reprocessing))

Overall, the evidence consistently shows EMDR significantly reduces PTSD symptoms and is endorsed by major clinical guidelines.
